Empirical Research Plan: “Does Economic Growth Reduce the Incidence of Civil Conflict in Sub-Saharan Africa?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
Strategy: Panel two–stage least squares (2SLS) / IV with country and year fixed effects.

Why IV?  
• Economic growth and conflict are jointly determined (reverse causality) and share unobserved drivers (institutions, geography).  
• Year-to-year rainfall variation is plausibly exogenous to political processes yet strongly affects (mainly rain-fed) agricultural income and hence GDP in the region.  
• A panel IV with fixed effects lets us difference out time-invariant country characteristics and common global shocks, isolating within-country, across-time variation in growth that is induced by weather.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
Treatment variable (endogenous regressor)  
 T_it  = real GDP per-capita growth rate (%) in country i, year t.

Instrument(s)  
 Z_it  = percentage change in annual rainfall relative to the previous year (current and possibly one-year lag).  
 Optional: use 12-month country-level log rainfall deviations from the 30-year mean.

Control group / counterfactual  
 There is no separate set of “untreated” units; all country-years form the panel. The counterfactual outcome for a given country-year is the conflict risk that would have prevailed at the (instrument-induced) GDP growth the country did not experience.

Timing  
 Strictly annual. The instrument is contemporaneous (and/or lagged) rainfall growth; T_it is same-year GDP growth; outcome is same-year (incidence) or next-year (onset) of civil conflict.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
A1 Relevance: Rainfall shocks substantially move GDP growth (first-stage F > 10).  
 Plausible: agriculture ≈40 % of SSA GDP; prior studies show elasticities 0.3–0.5.

A2 Exclusion (Instrumental Independence): Conditional on controls, rainfall affects civil conflict only through its impact on GDP.  
 Plausibility: Reasonable but not guaranteed—rainfall could influence fighting conditions or grievances directly. We will probe below.

A3 Exogeneity: Rainfall shocks are as-good-as-random with respect to unobserved determinants of conflict.  
 Plausible: Weather is unmanipulable; FE remove time-invariant geography; year FE capture continent-wide shocks.

A4 Monotonicity / no “defiers”: A positive rainfall shock never lowers income for any country-year through mechanisms other than agriculture (highly plausible).

A5 SUTVA / no cross-unit spillovers: Rainfall in country i does not directly alter conflict in country j once common shocks are netted out (relatively plausible given national borders; we will cluster SEs two-ways or at regional level as a precaution).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Remedies
Threat 1: Direct effect of rainfall on conflict (violates exclusion).  
 Remedies:  
 a. Control directly for rainfall level and its square (only growth is the instrument).  
 b. Use lagged rainfall growth as instrument, leaving a temporal gap (rainfall_{t-1} → GDP_t → conflict_t).  
 c. Conduct placebo tests on conflict‐irrelevant outcomes (e.g., UN voting patterns).

Threat 2: Weak instrument in non-agricultural economies or in oil exporters.  
 Remedies:  
 a. Report first-stage F-statistics and the Kleibergen-Paap rk Wald F.  
 b. Interact rainfall with agricultural share, or drop oil exporters in robustness.  
 c. Limited-information-max-likelihood (LIML) and Anderson-Rubin confidence sets.

Threat 3: Dynamic feedback—conflict persistence mechanically raises next-year conflict probability, potentially biasing standard errors and masking growth effects.  
 Remedies:  
 a. Include lagged conflict status as control.  
 b. Estimate separate models for onset (new wars) and incidence.  
 c. Cluster SEs at country level and allow for AR(1) autocorrelation (e.g., Driscoll-Kraay).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
```r
#------------------------------------------
# Required packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast feols / iv
library(lmtest)      # for weak-IV diagnostics
library(sandwich)

#------------------------------------------
# 1. Data loading
d <- read_csv("ssa_panel_1981_1999.csv")

#------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
d <- d %>% 
  mutate(
    ln_gdp_pc  = log(gdp_pc_const),
    gdp_grow   = 100*(ln_gdp_pc - lag(ln_gdp_pc)),      # Δln y
    rain_grow  = 100*(log(rainfall_mm) - lag(log(rainfall_mm))),
    lag_rain   = lag(rain_grow),
    conflict_inc  = if_else(battles_yr >= 25, 1, 0),    # incidence
    conflict_on   = if_else(conflict_inc == 1 & lag(conflict_inc)==0,1,0),
    log_pop    = log(pop),
    oil        = if_else(oil_exporter==1,1,0)
  ) %>% 
  group_by(country) %>% 
  mutate(country_trend = row_number()) %>% 
  ungroup()

#------------------------------------------
# 3. Main specification: 2SLS with FE
#   conflict incidence in year t on GDP growth (instrumented by rainfall growth)
iv_formula <- conflict_inc ~ gdp_grow + 
                           polity + ethn_frac + log_pop + mountains + oil |
                           lag_rain + polity + ethn_frac + log_pop + mountains + oil

est_main <- feols(
  formula = iv_formula,
  data    = d,
  fixef   = ~country + year,
  cluster = ~country
)

summary(est_main, stage = 1)   # shows both stages & F-stat

#------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness check:  a) country-specific trends; 
#                       b) drop oil exporters
est_trend <- feols(iv_formula, data = d,
                   fixef = ~country + year + country_trend,
                   cluster = ~country)

est_nooil <- feols(iv_formula, data = filter(d, oil==0),
                   fixef = ~country + year,
                   cluster = ~country)

etable(est_main, est_trend, est_nooil, stats = "n")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
Theory (opportunity cost) predicts a negative effect: positive income shocks lower the likelihood of civil conflict. Based on existing elasticities:

A 5 percentage-point increase in real GDP per-capita growth should reduce the probability of conflict incidence by roughly 1 percentage point (−0.20 ppt per 1 pp growth). For conflict onset, the magnitude may be slightly smaller (−0.12 ppt per 1 pp growth) but still negative.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
C1 Instrument relevance (first-stage strength)................. 1  
C2 Instrument exogeneity (uncorrelated with ε)................. 0.5  
C3 Exclusion restriction (no direct effect on Y)............... 0.5  
C4 Monotonicity (no defiers)................................... 1  
C5 Correct functional form & SUTVA / no spillovers............. 0.5  
Overall IV validity score: 3.5 / 5.
